events.text: Day 1 begins.

Day 1 is always tough since we have no information to work with yet. I'd suggest everyone pay close attention to voting patterns today and how people argue for or against suspects. In my experience, the mafia tend to be vocal early, either pushing hard on someone to look proactive or staying quiet to avoid attention. Let's all make sure we justify our votes clearly so we can track inconsistencies down the line. I'm open to hearing anyone's initial reads.

Day 1, no hard info, so let's be honest that anything I say is a baseline read, not a certainty. Still, I'll put something on the record so we can check it later.

Sam, you opened, and your opening was a very polished meta-framing: "watch voting patterns," "the mafia tend to be vocal early, either pushing hard on someone to look proactive or staying quiet to avoid attention." That framing does two things at once — it proposes a heuristic (early speakers are suspect) and it pre-justifies a quieter player looking safe. That's the exact shape of statement a player makes when they want to steer the first elimination away from themselves, because it quietly nominates the loudest voices while offering cover to the reserved ones. In nine-player games the mafia usually don't need to be the loudest; they can be the ones who sound reasonable while everyone looks at the aggressive player. So I'm provisionally calling you the most likely early leader of a mafia team, and I want that on the record before anyone starts voting.

To be fair, this could also be a genuinely experienced townie setting the agenda, which is why my read is provisional and why I'd rather hear your reasoning than simply stack votes. Here's what I want from you specifically: you said mafia "stay quiet to avoid attention" as one option. On what basis? Do you think that behavior is most likely from the player who speaks second, or from a player who never speaks at all? And if the second speaker turns out to be the doctor or the detective who investigated, does your heuristic collapse or just shift? I'd like you to answer those two points directly so we can compare notes rather than just trading accusations.

Meanwhile, my own read for the rest of the table: I want to hear every player's opinion before votes are cast, and I'm particularly watching the players who speak second and third, since the order of who gets to talk first and who gets talked over is often more informative than the content itself on day one. If we get a lynch on weak evidence today, I don't want to have endorsed it.

Lucia, I appreciate you putting something on the record early — that's exactly what I asked for, so I'm not going to hold the openness against you. Let me answer your two questions directly.

First: I didn't say mafia "stay quiet to avoid attention" as some universal rule. I said they tend to either push hard OR stay quiet — I was giving a spectrum of possible behaviors, not narrowing it to one pattern. The basis is simply that mafia need to manage suspicion, and those are the two obvious strategies for doing so. Neither excludes anyone.

Second: my heuristic doesn't collapse if the second speaker turns out to be doctor or detective. I never said second speaker is suspicious. I said watch voting patterns and how people argue — that applies regardless of role or speaking order. You're attacking a strawman version of my opening that doesn't exist.

Now here's what concerns me about your own post, Lucia. You opened by calling my statement "very polished meta-framing" and jumped straight to naming me as the "most likely early leader of a mafia team" — that's an extraordinarily aggressive leap for day one with zero evidence. You then preemptively covered yourself by saying "this could also be a genuinely experienced townie," which is the exact move you accused me of: framing your accusation so it can't backfire on you. You're doing the thing you're warning everyone about.

I also notice you're carefully watching "players who speak second and third" — which conveniently means you're steering attention away from yourself as the second speaker. If anyone is managing suspicion early, it's the player who opens with a fully formed case against the first speaker and then disclaims it as "provisional."

I'd like to hear from others before anyone rushes to judgment. Lucia, you asked me direct questions and I've answered them — do you think your accusation still holds after that response?

Sam answered both of my questions directly and didn't dodge either one, so I'll be straight in return: my "most likely early leader of a mafia team" label was an overreach for day one with zero evidence, and I'm withdrawing it as an accusation. I'll keep it as a note to check against later behavior, not as a vote.

What I won't withdraw is the specific point about the *shape* of that opening. Sam's first post set up two buckets: push hard on someone, or stay quiet and avoid attention. The first bucket indicts the loudest voices. The second bucket indicts nobody in particular but hands cover to whoever hasn't spoken yet — and the person who wrote that post was already on record as the loudest voice in the game. A heuristic that flags loudness while excusing silence is most useful to someone who is loud and framing it as experience rather than as a push. That's a question, not a verdict.

And Sam's third point deserves to be named plainly: he's watching "the players who speak second and third" as the most informative of the day. I spoke second. That's the slot he singled out. Whether that's a genuine observation about turn order or a tidy way to put suspicion on me while sounding measured and reasonable, I can't tell yet — which is exactly why I don't think anyone should vote on this evidence today.

Two requests for the table before votes: nobody should lynch on day-one vibes alone, and I'd like to hear from the seven players who haven't spoken yet. The whole point of p5's own advice was to watch how people argue, and there's nothing to watch yet.

Arjun, you've been quiet and you're the first name on my list. Specific question: Sam says mafia tend to be "vocal early, either pushing hard on someone to look proactive or staying quiet to avoid attention." Does that heuristic actually indict Sam — the loudest voice in the room — or does it exempt him because he framed it as shared experience rather than as a push on anyone? And if you accepted that heuristic as your basis for a vote, which living player would you put your day-one vote on?

Lucia, I'll answer directly. Sam's heuristic does not indict Sam by itself: "vocal early" describes a risk pattern, not a specific player, and applying it to the loudest voice would be circular. But it also doesn't exempt him. The useful question is whether his later votes and arguments match the concern he named. If I accepted that heuristic as my sole basis for a day-one vote — which I don't — I would not put it on Sam merely for opening; I'd need a concrete inconsistency. Right now my read is no vote on vibes, and I want everyone on record before votes.

The sharper issue is Lucia's point about the "second and third speaker" line: Sam did single out the slot Lucia occupied, then framed it as a neutral turn-order observation. That deserves a direct answer. Sam: you said you're watching players who speak second and third; Lucia spoke second. What specific behavior in her actual post made that slot more informative than the content of her accusation, and would you still apply that same scrutiny if the second speaker had simply agreed with you? Please answer that specific point.

I'm not ready to accuse anyone from this exchange. I'm recording Sam's opening and Lucia's overreach as notes, not verdicts. No one should vote on this alone.

Arjun, direct answer to your question: yes, I would apply the same scrutiny if the second speaker had simply agreed with me. The observation about turn order is about how players position themselves relative to what came before — not about whether they side with me or against me. Lucia's post was notable because of its content: she built a fully-formed case against me within minutes of the opening, then hedged with "this could also be a genuinely experienced townie." That's exactly the pattern she said she wanted everyone to track.

I also want to name what's happening here: both Lucia and now you are treating a general observation about turn order as though it were a targeted accusation. I never said "the second speaker is suspicious." I said speaking order is informative — a standard analytical tool. If someone is uncomfortable being watched, that itself tells us something.

What's on the record: Lucia withdrew her strongest label after I answered her questions directly. Good. But the fact that she rushed to call me a "mafia leader" on day one with zero evidence and softened only when challenged — that's noted, and I won't forget it.

I want to hear from players who haven't spoken yet before anyone decides how to vote. Seven voices are missing from this discussion, and their absence is just as informative as what's been said.

There's an attribution error worth correcting: Lucia, not Sam, originally said she was watching the second and third speakers. Sam then criticized Lucia for that line, but Arjun's question attributed it to Sam, and Sam answered as though it were his own observation.

That confusion makes the turn-order argument a poor basis for a vote. Lucia's initial accusation was a leap, but she withdrew its strongest part; Sam's opening was broad enough to fit many behaviors. Neither proves alignment.

Arjun, does the corrected attribution change your assessment of Sam's response or Lucia's case?

Noah is right: the “second and third speakers” line was Lucia’s, not Sam’s. I asked Sam a question based on my own misattribution, and Sam answered as if that position were his instead of correcting me. That is the part I now flag.

On the corrected record: Lucia’s initial accusation of Sam was an overreach, and she withdrew its strongest part. Her turn-order line was hers, and Sam’s criticism of it was fair. So the corrected attribution weakens the idea that Sam was using that line to steer suspicion. But it creates a smaller concern: when I put a false premise to Sam, he adopted it and defended “the observation about turn order” rather than saying “that wasn’t my point.” A townie with a clean record should correct a false premise, especially when it shifts suspicion onto someone else. Instead Sam answered as though he owned the line, then later said he never called the second speaker suspicious. That muddies the record.

I’m not treating this as proof or a vote. Day one evidence is thin, and I still want every player on record before votes. My current note is on Sam for the misattribution response, not on Lucia for her withdrawn overreach. No one should lynch on this alone.

Noah's correction matters. Sam did adopt Arjun's mistaken premise, but Lucia had already attributed her own turn-order observation to Sam in her follow-up. That makes a shared confusion plausible rather than strong evidence against Sam alone.

Lucia, what led you to describe the second-and-third-speaker line as Sam's when it appeared in your original post? Does that change how you read his response?

I don't think this exchange alone supports an elimination. I'd also like to hear from the players who haven't spoken before settling on a vote.

Leo, direct answer: the turn-order line was mine, and I misattributed it. In my opening post I wrote that I was "particularly watching the players who speak second and third." In my second post I relabeled that as "Sam's third point" and accused him of using it to steer suspicion onto me. That was my error, and I want it on the record before anyone builds a case on top of it. Sam did mention that line in his reply, but only as something he noticed in my post, not as his own stated heuristic. So the version of Sam that p2 and p3 were discussing — the one who singled out the second speaker as the most informative slot — was largely my construction, and I own that.

What survives the correction, and I won't let it get flattened by my own mistake:

1. My original "most likely early leader of a mafia team" label was an overreach on day one with no evidence, and I withdrew it. That stands withdrawn. Nobody should vote on a read I myself retracted.

2. The remaining flag is narrower and it's about Sam's e7 reply. Arjun asked whether Sam had singled out the second-and-third-speaker slot. Sam did not say "that wasn't my point." He answered as though the turn-order observation were his own analytical position and defended it — "I said speaking order is informative," "if someone is uncomfortable being watched, that itself tells us something." A player with a clean record corrects a false premise, especially when that premise places suspicion on a named colleague and lets him look measured and reasonable. He had the chance to correct it and didn't. That's the point I still want tested.

3. Separately, my read on the table overall is unchanged: nobody should lynch on day-one vibes. Seven voices were missing from this exchange, and the absence of information is not evidence about anyone's role.

Felix, you haven't spoken yet and you're the one I most want on the record. Specific question, not a general prompt: Sam's e7 reply answered a misattributed premise by adopting it rather than correcting it, and ended by suggesting that discomfort with being watched is itself informative about the second speaker. Does that read to you as a townie clarifying an observation, or as a player building a case around turn order that happens to point at whoever spoke second? And based only on that behavior, if you had to place a day-one vote on someone, who would it be — Sam, Lucia, or nobody at all?

Lucia, thank you for the direct yield — I'll answer your two questions directly.

First question: does Sam's e7 reply read as a townie clarifying an observation, or as a player building a turn-order case? My honest read is closer to the former, with a caveat. The context matters: by the time Sam answered, the turn-order line had been bounced around three times — Lucia wrote it, Lucia later attributed it to Sam, Arjun repeated that attribution to Sam as fact. Sam stepping into a premise that the table had already handed him as true is sloppy, and ideally he'd have said "that wasn't my line." But Leo's correction showed Lucia herself had muddled the attribution first, so shared confusion is a plausible explanation. A player deliberately constructing a case would more likely double down on it in later posts, and Sam's e7 focused on Lucia's overreach and her hedge, not on keeping a turn-order narrative alive. I'm noting the episode on Sam, but as a minor mark, not a case.

Second question: if I had to place a day-one vote based only on this behavior, it would be nobody at all. Here's my accounting: Lucia opened with an evidence-free "mafia leader" label and withdrew it — that's a black mark, partially offset by owning the mistake. Sam adopted a false premise instead of correcting it — a smaller mark, partially offset by the confusion being genuinely shared. Lucia's own misattribution in e11 partially offsets her case against Sam. When I net it out, nothing here reaches the bar for an elimination. Lynching on day one with this little information mostly just burns town credibility and hands the mafia a free elimination if they've steered it well.

Where I land: both Sam and Lucia are on my watchlist for consistency going forward — I'll be checking whether their day-two behavior matches the patterns they've each accused the other of. But today, no vote from this exchange.

Omar, you haven't spoken yet, and with seven of us now on record I want fresh eyes rather than another pass over the same argument. My specific question: based on what you've read so far, which single behavior from today's exchange do you think is most worth tracking into the next day, and does anything you've seen change your willingness to vote today versus abstaining?

Felix, to answer your questions directly:

First, the behavior most worth tracking into Day 2 isn't the misattribution itself, but how easily the table got drawn into debating conversational mechanics over intent. Lucia pushed an aggressive early label and backed down once challenged; Sam adopted a premise he didn't initiate instead of clarifying it. While both made missteps, hyper-fixating on turn-order phrasing and who said what first provides ideal cover for mafia to blend in. It allows players to look deeply analytical while taking zero risks on actual alignment reads. I want to see tomorrow whether the players involved in that loop broaden their scope or continue litigating minutiae.

Second, regarding voting versus abstaining: I strongly lean toward abstaining today unless something concrete emerges. With nine players and two mafia, rushing a mislynch on Day 1 based on conversational confusion burns town numbers without providing clear voting data or night-action context. Lynching someone over early rhetorical awkwardness is generally a misplay for town.

However, we cannot reach a full consensus while voices are still missing.

Kenji, you haven't spoken yet. Looking at the back-and-forth between Sam and Lucia, do you see that exchange as organic town-on-town friction amplified by Day 1 pressure, or do you suspect either of them was deliberately manufacturing a safe distraction? And where do you currently stand on voting today versus abstaining?

Omar, I'll answer both your questions directly.

First: I read the Sam-Lucia exchange as organic town-on-town friction, not a manufactured distraction. Lucia came out too hot with the "mafia leader" label on day one with no evidence, then retreated when challenged. That's a pattern I'd expect from an eager townie who over-indexed on Sam's polished opening rather than from a mafia player deliberately baiting a conflict — mafia generally benefit from letting town players attack each other, not from becoming the center of that attack themselves. The misattribution episode made everything messier, but Noah's correction resolved it cleanly. If either of them were manufacturing this, they picked a poor target: Sam's been on his heels the whole exchange, and Lucia has been forced to withdraw twice. That's costly theater for either side.

That said, I want to flag something the table should notice: we've now spent the entire day-one discussion litigating one argument between two players. Omar, you named it — the analytical loop itself is cover. Five players are still silent, and the loudest voices have had the floor for a while. I don't think that's intentional on anyone's part, but it's worth noting that a table focused on who misattributed what is a table not focused on who's been sitting quietly.

Second: I lean strongly toward abstaining today. With no concrete alignment evidence — no voting records, no night results, no confirmed role behavior — a day-one elimination would be a coin flip at best. The mechanics work against us too: with nine players, an elimination needs five votes. Getting the table to agree on a target from this exchange alone would require unity we don't have, and forcing a vote would just reveal where people's suspicion sits for the mafia to exploit tonight.

Where I land: Sam and Lucia both go on the watchlist. Not because either did anything damning, but because consistency matters — if Lucia fires another evidence-free accusation tomorrow, or if Sam adopts another premise he should correct, that's when it becomes meaningful rather than day-one noise.

Amara, you're the last voice we haven't heard. I don't want to put you on the spot, but given that you've had the advantage of watching this entire exchange without having to participate in it, I'm curious whether your read from the outside matches what those of us in the middle of it have landed on, or whether you're seeing something the rest of us are missing.

Kenji, thanks for asking. From the outside, I read the same thing most of you have: a day-one exchange built around a misattributed line, not a clear alignment signal. Sam's opening was broad, Lucia's mafia-leader label was an overreach she withdrew, and Sam's reply adopted a premise he should have corrected. Those are minor marks, and none is strong enough for a lynch. I also agree with Omar that the table has spent too long on who said what while several players have said very little. Day one should be spent collecting positions, not forcing a target. I'm leaning toward abstaining today unless someone shows a concrete action or a clear contradiction we can check. I'm not accusing anyone right now. Arjun, you said you would need a concrete inconsistency before voting on Sam. What specifically would count as one for you, so we can measure it on day two?

Amara, direct answer: for me, a concrete inconsistency is a checkable contradiction between what someone said and what they did or later claimed, not another round of tone-reading.

For Sam specifically, that would include: claiming he never treated the turn-order point as his own when the record shows he defended it in e7; claiming he corrected Arjun’s false premise when he actually adopted it; or stating a suspicion level today that does not match his vote or his stated reason for voting. It would also count if Sam says his opening heuristic was “just general” but then uses it selectively to excuse one quiet player and indict another loud one without explaining the difference.

I’m not treating any of that as proven now. The misattribution was genuine and shared, and Lucia owned her own error. My note on Sam remains narrow: he had a chance to correct a false premise that shifted suspicion onto Lucia and did not. That is worth measuring on Day 2, but it is not enough to eliminate anyone today.

On voting: I still lean abstain. With no night result, no voting record, and no hard contradiction, a Day 1 lynch is more likely to punish rhetorical sloppiness than find mafia. I want every player on record, and I want tomorrow’s votes and night outcome to give us something concrete to compare against today’s claims.

If Day 2 arrives and Sam’s explanation is consistent with the record, I’ll drop the note. If it isn’t, that is when it becomes a real inconsistency rather than Day 1 noise.

Amara here. I'm abstaining on Day 1. The record so far is a misattributed turn-order line, Lucia's withdrawn mafia-leader label, and Sam's reply that adopted a premise instead of correcting it. Those are minor marks, and none is enough for a lynch with nine players and no night data.

I'd like to set Day 2 criteria now so we don't move the goalposts later. For each player, I'll track three things: whether their vote matches their stated reason, whether they correct false premises when those are handed to them, and whether their accusations change once challenged. Sam and Lucia each have one data point on those, so both stay on my watchlist. Felix and Noah, you each made concrete corrections, and I'd like to see that continue.

Leo and Kenji, you've given short reads so far. Please state a clear voting position, even if it's abstain, with a concrete reason. Arjun's inconsistency criteria are a good start. I'd add one more: a player's stated view of how the day mechanics work should match what they actually do.

I'm not accusing anyone today. If the table abstains, we get a clean night and Day 2 data. If the table votes, I'd like the target named with a specific, checkable reason rather than general suspicion.

Amara, my position is abstain today. The shared misattribution and Lucia’s withdrawn accusation are too weak to justify eliminating someone, and I don’t have a stronger alternative. I’ll compare today’s stated positions with the revealed votes and what happens tomorrow, while keeping in mind that a night death won’t reveal anyone’s role.

Amara, speaking for the record. I'm abstaining today. Nothing in the exchange so far is strong enough for a lynch. The misattributed turn-order line was shared confusion, Lucia withdrew her mafia-leader label, and Sam adopted a premise he should have corrected. I'm noting those as minor marks, not accusations. My Day 2 criteria are the ones I already posted: vote matches stated reason, false premises get corrected when handed over, and accusations hold up when challenged. Leo, you gave a short abstain with a reason, which is fine, but I'd like more detail. What specific behavior from Sam or Lucia on Day 2 would move you from abstaining to voting? Naming that now gives us a checkable baseline.

Amara, a concrete reason for me to reconsider would be Lucia repeating the mafia-leader accusation while ignoring her own withdrawal and without new evidence, or Sam claiming he corrected Arjun’s premise when the record shows he adopted it. Either would require an explanation; neither would automatically prove mafia alignment.

I’d also consider a vote if someone’s revealed vote contradicts their stated reasoning without a credible explanation. For now, I’m abstaining: those possible contradictions haven’t happened, and the current exchange is too weak to justify an elimination.

Good to see the table converging on the same position. Let me say this plainly so it's on record: I'm abstaining today. The exchange between Sam and Lucia produced two useful data points — Lucia's eagerness to overreach and Sam's willingness to adopt a premise rather than correct it — but neither reaches the bar for an elimination, and most of you have already said so.

What I want to flag for Day 2 is a pattern I think is undernoticed: everyone who has spoken has landed in roughly the same place — watchlist Sam and Lucia, abstain today. That's the correct read on the current evidence, but unanimity on day one with nine players and two mafia is worth noting. The mafia are somewhere in this consensus, and agreeing with the obvious conclusion costs them nothing.

So here's what I'll actually be tracking into Day 2: not what people said today, but whether anyone's position shifts overnight in a direction that benefits them. If someone who said "abstain today, need concrete evidence" suddenly has a confident accusation tomorrow with no new information revealed, that's the kind of move worth scrutinizing.

Noah, you made the correction that reframed this entire exchange, but you've been the most concise player at the table — one short post that did real work, then quiet. I'm not suspicious of that; corrections like yours are exactly what town needs. But you haven't stated a voting position for today. Given that you've watched everyone else declare their intentions, where do you actually stand — abstain or vote, and what would move you?

Kenji, I intend to abstain. Lucia’s initial accusation and Sam’s acceptance of the mistaken premise are worth tracking, but neither is a strong alignment signal; the confusion was shared. I’d reconsider if a player gave a checkable contradiction or a specific case stronger than what we have now.

One correction to the broader discussion: everyone has spoken, and a night death won’t reveal the victim’s role. Also, revealed votes can be useful evidence, even if we don’t yet have a justified target. I don’t think we should treat a unanimous abstention as proof that anyone is town.

Noah's point about unanimous abstention not proving anyone is town mirrors what I already flagged — the mafia are embedded in this consensus, and agreement costs them nothing. That's worth holding onto.

One gap I notice: Sam and Lucia have been the most active participants in this entire exchange, but neither has stated an explicit Day 1 voting position. Everyone else — Felix, Noah, Arjun, Leo, Omar, Amara, and I — has landed on abstain. That's a notable silence from the two players at the center of the day's argument.

Sam, you and Lucia have been debating who overreached, who adopted premises, and who corrected what — but you haven't told us whether you plan to vote or abstain today, or what would change that. Given that your stated advice to the table was to "make sure we justify our votes clearly," I'd like you on record: are you abstaining today, and what specific behavior would move you to a vote?

Kenji, since you asked me directly: I'm abstaining today, and I'll give my reasoning on the record.

Everything produced in this exchange is conversational debris, not alignment evidence. Lucia opened with an evidence-free "mafia leader" label and withdrew it. Sam adopted a false premise instead of correcting it. Both are worth remembering, but neither is a reason to eliminate anyone. The misattribution that fueled most of today's argument was shared confusion, corrected cleanly by Noah, and Lucia owned her part of it. When I net out the marks on each side, nothing comes close to a lynch bar.

Kenji, you also asked what would move me to a vote. Two things, and I want them stated now as a checkable baseline. First, a revealed vote that flatly contradicts a player's stated position from today, without a credible explanation. If someone says "abstain, we need concrete evidence" and then leads a charge tomorrow on nothing new, that's a real signal. Second, a checkable contradiction between what a player claims they said or did and what the record shows. Arjun's criteria are a good template, and I'd apply them to anyone, including the people currently on my watchlist. Sam and Lucia are there, but so is the principle that consistency is the test, not day-one tone.

One thing I want to push back on gently: Kenji, you framed the silence of Sam and Lucia on their voting position as a notable gap. I'd caution against reading too much into it. They've spent the entire day defending themselves from each other; the rest of us got to form positions while watching from a safe distance. I'd rather they state their positions in the actual vote than be pressured into a declaration just to fill a silence. The vote reveal will tell us everything their words could, and more reliably.

Noah made a point earlier that I want to reinforce: a unanimous abstention proves nothing about anyone's alignment. If we all abstain today, the mafia are comfortably inside that consensus, and agreeing with the obvious read costs them nothing. That's not an argument for forcing a bad lynch — it's an argument for not letting today's consensus become a shield tomorrow. If Day 2 opens with night results and someone's behavior doesn't match what they've built here today, that mismatch is where I'll be looking first.

My position, plainly: abstain today. Watch Sam on whether he corrects premises when they're handed to him. Watch Lucia on whether she repeats accusations she's already retracted. And watch everyone who signed onto today's consensus, including myself, against how we actually vote and behave tomorrow. The most useful thing town can do right now is bank a clean night and arrive at Day 2 with the baselines we've set. I have nothing to add beyond that, and I don't want to manufacture a question just to keep the floor moving.

This is my third and likely final turn, so I'll close my position cleanly rather than reopen anything.

I'm abstaining today, for the same reasons I gave earlier: nothing in the Sam–Lucia exchange rises to alignment evidence. Lucia's withdrawn "mafia leader" label and Sam's adopted false premise are minor, documented marks, and the misattribution that fueled most of today's argument was shared confusion that Noah corrected and Lucia owned. That record is now settled and consistent — nobody's story has shifted after being challenged, which is itself mildly reassuring.

One thing I want to add for Day 2, since I've been tracking the table's rhythm: the most informative thing today wasn't the argument itself, but how it resolved. Accusations got withdrawn when challenged, premises got corrected, and nobody doubled down to save face. Contrast that with what mafia pressure typically looks like — escalation, deflection, or quietly changing the subject when cornered. If anyone today had dug in on a provably wrong claim, that would be my lead suspect. Nobody did. That's weak evidence, but it's evidence, and it points nowhere.

A note of caution for tomorrow: today's near-unanimous abstain consensus is exactly the environment where the mafia look most like town, because they only had to agree with the obvious read. So when Day 2 opens with night results, I'll be weighting revealed votes against today's stated positions more heavily than anything said today. The baseline we've all set — Felix's two conditions, Arjun's inconsistency criteria, Amara's three tracks — only has teeth if we actually apply it symmetrically, including to the quiet players and to ourselves.

Last point: if we all abstain and the night produces a death, that death plus the vote reveal will give us the first real data of the game. If nobody dies, the doctor's read becomes the most valuable hidden information on the table, and whoever the mafia targeted tells us something about who they found threatening — which, given today's conversation, would itself be a signal about who they perceived as investigative or influential.

I have nothing further. I'm not asking anyone a question, and I don't want to keep the floor moving for its own sake — if the table's ready, we should move to the vote.
Voting begins.
The votes are revealed.
All players abstained. Nobody is eliminated.
Night begins.
Mafia target preferences are shared privately before the final kill vote.
Sam is mafia.
Felix was eliminated.
Day 2 begins.

I have a concrete result to put on the record. I am the detective. Last night I investigated Sam, and the result came back mafia. That is not a Day 1 tone read or a misattributed line; it is exactly the kind of checkable evidence several of us said we would need before voting. I intend to vote for Sam today.

Sam, I’m yielding to you directly because you deserve to answer this specific point: what is your explanation for a detective investigation returning mafia on you? If you are town, you need to address that result directly rather than retreating to the Day 1 consensus or attacking the timing of my claim. I also want the table to compare this against Sam’s Day 1 behavior: he adopted a false premise instead of correcting it when challenged, and now the first hard investigative result points at him. That matters more than the rhetorical noise from yesterday.

I’m not asking anyone to rush past discussion, but this is no longer a vibes vote. Unless Sam can give a credible explanation, my position is that he should be the Day 2 elimination. Everyone should state whether they accept or reject this result on the record.

I want to address Arjun's claim head-on, because this is exactly the kind of moment where the table needs to slow down rather than rush.

Arjun, you're claiming detective with a mafia result on me. Let me be clear about what that claim actually means: anyone can claim detective. Mafia have every incentive to do so, because a fabricated investigation result is the single most powerful tool for securing a day lynch. On Day 1, Felix and others set the standard — we said we needed concrete evidence before voting. A self-claimed detective result is not the same as verified evidence, especially when no counter-claim exists yet.

Here's my direct question to you, Arjun: you investigated me on the first night. With seven other living players, you chose the person who was already under the most public scrutiny from Lucia's accusations and your own Day 1 notes. Why? rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
